title: Emotions in Negotiation
description: Anger, anxiety, disappointment, and excitement systematically change what you demand, what you concede, and when you walk away.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Anger, anxiety, disappointment, and excitement systematically change what you demand, what you concede, and when you walk away.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: An anxious candidate accepts the first offer without countering.
A buyer who appears disappointed ('I really expected a better number based on our history') triggers concession without aggression.
An angry supplier demands more but gets counter-anger if the other side has equal power.

sections.title: Real Examples of Strategic Emotion
content: Slight, genuine disappointment after an offer: pause, small sigh, 'Hm, that's lower than I was hoping.' Then silence. Often prompts a raise.
Feigned anger rarely works; it's usually detectable and backfires.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You feel a sudden urge to concede just to end the discomfort.
You're making decisions faster than usual because your heart is racing.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
sections.content: If you feel strong emotion during a negotiation, call a break. Say, 'Let me take a few minutes to think this through.' Never decide in an emotional spike.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Emotions are data, not directives. Use them as signals, not decision-makers.
